title: Contingency pathways: node bypass and GPU rollforward (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This draft runbook captures an operational pattern were calling node-bypass + GPU rollforward: a safe, staged set of actions to keep inference capacity online while performing disruptive maintenance (accelerator replacement, kernel updates, firmware patches) or when troubleshooting node-level GPU faults. Its intended for on-call SREs and infra engineers responsible for cluster stability during GPU-related incidents.

Scope / when to use:
- Detected GPU hardware degradation (ECC errors, persistent TDRs, kernel oopses tied to accel).
- Node-level driver instability impacting one or two GPUs but where pod evacuation would cause service-level degradation.
- Planned maintenance windows where a subset of GPUs on a node will be replaced or firmware updated and we want graceful capacity preservation.
- NOT for full-node unrecoverable failures; for those use the standard cordon/drain -> node replacement workflow.

High-level strategy (why this pattern helps):
1) Temporarily bypass the affected GPU(s) at the scheduler/runtime level so workloads continue on remaining healthy GPUs or nodes.
2) Inject temporary capacity or route live traffic to compatible model variants (smaller batch or quantized) to preserve p99 latency SLOs.
3) Execute physical replacement or software-level rollforward on a staggered, low-risk schedule.
4) Validate end-to-end inference correctness and performance, then re-introduce the GPU into rotation.

Key benefits:
- Reduced blast radius versus cordon-and-drain of entire node.
- Faster mean time to recovery for partial GPU faults.
- Clear rollback path and metrics to validate safety.

Quick checklist (on-call immediate actions):
- Triage: collect node and GPU identifiers (kubectl get nodes, nvidia-smi).
- Quarantine: add GPU to scheduler blacklist or set node annotation to avoid scheduling onto affected GPU index.
- Capacity: verify cluster spare capacity or provision emergency burst nodes.
- Route: enable model fallback routing to compatible variant if latency rising.
- Replace or patch: perform GPU replacement/driver update on a per-GPU staged basis.
- Validate and re-enable GPU.

Detailed run steps (staging + emergency):
1) Initial triage (5-10 min)
   - Identify node and GPU index: ssh to node or use kube-node-exporter/GPU exporter.
     - kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces | grep <node-name>
     - ssh node: sudo nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,uuid,temperature.gpu,fan.speed,retired
   - Check logs: journalctl -u kubelet -n 200, dmesg | tail -n 200, /var/log/messages, driver logs (/var/log/nvidia-installer.log)
   - Open a Jira/incident record if not open. Link to slack: #sre-gpu-incidents.

2) Immediate mitigation: scheduler-level bypass (10-20 min)
   Option A (preferred if runtime supports per-GPU routing): use the inference runtimes GPU mask feature to mark GPU index as unavailable.
     - Example runtime API: POST /runtime/nodes/<node>/gpus/mask {"mask": "0b0111011"} (mask bits 0=available, 1=masked) -- refer to runtime API doc.
   Option B (k8s-level annotation): set node annotation to instruct device-plugin to advertise only healthy GPUs.
     - kubectl annotate node <node-name> gpu/inventory-mask="exclude=1,3" --overwrite
     - rollout restart daemonset/nvidia-device-plugin -n kube-system (if needed)
   Option C (pod eviction for pods pinned to faulty GPU): scale down specific DaemonSet pods pinned to GPU index and allow scheduler to reschedule to other nodes.

   Notes: Document which method used in the incident ticket. If device-plugin behavior is unclear, prefer annotations over daemon restarts in production.

3) Capacity stabilization (15-60 min)
   - Check available capacity: Grafana panel: cluster/gpu/available-count. Prometheus query: sum(kube_node_status_allocatable_gpu) - sum(gpu_allocated_tokens)
   - If capacity < threshold (configured per-customer): trigger emergency capacity pipeline:
     - Terraform apply (staging credentials): modules/gpu-pool/auto-burst -var emergency=true -target=module.pool
     - Or in cloud console, spin up pre-baked GPU instance (g4dn/g5 or whatever our build uses). Tag as ephemeral.
   - Re-route traffic via smart routing policy: set routing policy weight for model variants in console to shift 25-50% to cheaper/compatible variants while keeping majority on production.

4) Safe rollforward (scheduled work window)
   - Prepare: ensure spare node or empty GPU available for warm-up. Notify stakeholders (channel + incident ticket + ops calendar).
   - Drain only affected GPU (physical or virtual): if performing a hardware swap, follow physical replacement SOP (EHS, rack access, ESD, label replacement GPU with node/gpu-index). For driver/firmware updates, coordinate kernel/drivers versions.
   - When replacing hardware: perform replacement on one GPU at a time. After each replacement: power on, run health checks below.

5) Health checks to re-enable GPU (post-change validation)
   System-level checks (run on node):
     - sudo nvidia-smi -q | grep -E "Error|Retired|Pending"
     - check dmesg for nouveau/nvidia errors in last 5 mins: dmesg --ctime | tail -n 200 | egrep -i "nvrm|nvidia|gpu|nouveau"
   Runtime-level checks:
     - Run a smoke inference on the runtime that pins to the newly enabled GPU: curl -sS -X POST $RUNTIME/smoke -d '{"model":"smoke-bert","gpu":<index>,"batch":1,"input":"quick test"}'
     - Verify latency p50/p95 within baseline and no OOM errors.
   Cluster-level checks:
     - Prometheus queries: increase in gpu_allocated_tokens should match expected. Error rates: rate(runtime_errors_total[2m]) should not spike.
   If checks pass, unmask GPU and allow scheduler to place pods. If any check fails, revert to bypass and escalate to hardware vendor.

6) Rollback path (always prepare in parallel)
   - If re-enabling GPU causes latency/incorrect outputs, immediately re-mask the GPU with the same mechanism used to bypass.
   - If behavior persists after revert, mark node for offline replacement and migrate workloads: kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force
   - Shift traffic to reserved capacity pool and notify customer success if customer-visible.

Monitoring and key signals to watch (Dashboard checklist):
- Cluster SLOs: p99 latency, 5xx rate, error-rate by model.
- Node-level: GPU Retired/Remap counters, ECC errors, temperature spikes. Prometheus queries:
  - sum by(node) (nvidia_gpu_ecc_errors_total)
  - rate(runtime_errors_total[1m])
  - sum(cluster_gpu_available) - expected_capacity
- Cost/usage: monitor emergency-burst instances usage and tags to ensure we cleanup after.

Communication templates (slack + incident ticket):
- Slack status update (short): "SRE: ongoing GPU incident on node <node-name>. Bypassed GPU #<index> at 13:24. Traffic shifted to variant-quantized (20%). Provisioning +2 GPU nodes for burst. ETA replacement window: 45m. Follow ticket INC-778 for details."
- Post-reenable update: "Reenabled GPU #<index> on <node>. Smoke checks passed: p50 unchanged, p95 +2ms. Monitoring for 30m before auto-unmasking."

Post-incident checklist (for retrospective and handoff):
- Capture timeline: detection -> mask -> capacity -> replace -> validate -> re-enable.
- Collect artifacts: node logs (dmesg, kubelet), runtime traces, Grafana snapshots, packet captures if needed. Attach to incident ticket.
- RCA triggers: if repeated ECC/retirement events on same hardware model or firmware version, open hardware vendor case and flag for fleet-wide mitigation.
- Cleanup: deprovision emergency nodes, remove temporary routing overrides, update capacity budgets.

Operational notes / things Ive noticed in prior incidents (notes to self):
- Device-plugin restarts can cause flapping with eviction storms; avoid if possible. Using node annotations + runtime mask has lower churn.
- Some pods are pinned to GPU indices via local-devices; have a checklist earlier to locate them and handle explicitly.
- Avoid simultaneous multi-GPU reboots on the same node; stagger at least 5-10 minutes between re-enables to let KV caches rebuild.
- When doing firmware updates, check for microcode/kernel compatibility matrix - vendor docs often list a specific kernel+driver combination.

TODOs (future improvements):
- Implement an automated 'gpu-bypass' orchestration play in the control plane so on-call can click a single button that performs mask + capacity check + routing shift.
- Add a small 'canary workload' job that runs on newly-enabled GPUs automatically for 10 minutes before full traffic.
- Add a Grafana alert that requires a human to acknowledge when GPUs are masked for >60m.

Appendix: quick commands reference
- List pods on node: kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node-name>
- Query GPU status: ssh <node> sudo nvidia-smi -q -x
- Mask via annotation: kubectl annotate node <node> gpu/inventory-mask="exclude=<indices>" --overwrite
- Cordon and drain (if escalated): kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force
- Provision emergency node (GCP example): gcloud compute instances create gpu-burst-01 --machine-type=a2-highgpu-1g --accelerator=type=nvidia-a100,count=1 --image-family=redwood-gpu --scopes=cloud-platform --tags=emergency-burst

Owner notes: this is a working doc. Please add specific runtime API snippets and a short runbook play UI prototype once the control plane route is implemented. Save logs under incident folder and link back here.

Last reviewed by: Miguel Ortega (2025-01-08)
